entry.title: ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement
entry.summary: Yoju Matsubayashi's latest film follows third-generation Okinawan-Brazilian as they reflect on their distant homeland.
entry.content:
The Kasato Maru ferried 325 Okinawans to Brazil in 1908, making it the first immigrant ship from Japan to do so. That history is highlighted by the opening of the documentary “Okinawa Saudade,” (“saudade” being a Portuguese word for bittersweet longing, typically around a memory or place). The film looks at the results a century later, now that an estimated 200,000 Brazilians of Okinawan descent are living in Brazil today, and director and cinematographer Yoju Matsubayashi finds a specific and emotionally straightforward route into complicated history. The director has covered the subject to some extent before in 2020’s “Okinawa / Santos,” a film which collected testimony on the forced deportation and even internment of Japanese immigrants in Brazil in the 1940s.””Okinawa Saudade”” narrows that focus to the families of two third-generation Okinawan-Brazilians, specifically ones with an interest in — and a longing towards — the island their families came from, something partially explored through the arts.

Related Stories
AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them
The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

A visual motif of waves viewed from above punctuates different segments of the film, typically as its subject reflect on the previous movements of their families. In the first instance of the shot, a dissolve to a young girl practicing a traditional Japanese dance on her family’s farm in Brazil immediately communicates that feeling of “saudade,” a soft and gently expressed shadow hanging over much of the film. That feeling of “saudade” is seen in the incidental details the director chooses to include, like how one subject’s grandfather grew dragonfruit with Okinawan seeds, as well as his capturing of more outwardly emotional moments, like a tearful reaction to photos not seen in a long time.

The teenage girl Yumi practices Ryukyu Buyo, while a man named Everton practices Eisa, an Okinawan folk dance involving drums. By unspooling their enthusiasm for the history of such Okinawan heritage arts and the history of their families, Matsubayashi also orbits a history of displacement. This emerges in an accumulation of lots of small personal stories, like how one characters recounts their family’s war-motivated exile from Santos. Yumi and Everton also learn more of these details for themselves, the film following them on their travels to Okinawa through exchange programs and traineeships. (In some delightful cases, the learning cuts both ways, as Everton reunites with estranged family, and Yumi’s Okinawan relative marvels at the dialect being preserved halfway around the world.)

Capturing their subjects’ respective journeys with occasional and mostly spontaneous interviews, Matsubayashi prioritizes personal histories over the big picture,as the assembly of the footage and the occasional interjection of archival material makes the relationship of this diaspora a bit clearer. Some of these families left Okinawa to avoid the military draft as well as starvation. Others were divided because of land seizures by the US military in the wake of the war (“I’ve learned that this is a sad place,” Yumi reflects, a quote placed over footage of lingering American military bases on the island). Some viewers might be dissatisfied with how Matsubayashi never quite engages with World War II and the full history of Okinawan annexation directly, but the context feels like plenty for the stories which he is telling, choosing instead to focus on the feelings which all children of immigrant backgrounds have felt: an uncertainty about their connection with the homeland of their parents and grandparents, and a yearning to understand it. The glimpses are enough, as “Okinawa Saudade”gradually paints a picture of how the historical struggles of the island have translated to the diaspora.

Everton outright says why he engages in Eisa drumming, saying that “we are Brazilians, but we don’t look like Brazilians, so we are always looking for belonging,” and his engagement with these traditional artforms becomes a part of this. Both learn the different nuances of their respective practices at home compared to in Okinawa, though both are graced with teachers who refuse to be super didactic about what is “authentic” (“We are always adjusting,” Yumi’s teacher says, “there is no such thing as perfection”). It’s also simply moving seeing, through Matsubayashi’s rather unvarnished camerawork, how the connections and feelings embodied in performing arts can have such far reach across time and place, highlighting the community found by the Brazilian Okinawans who preserved a little piece of the island for themselves.

Grade: B+

“Okinawa Saudade” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

entry.title: AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them
entry.summary: A week after partnering on our Future of Filmmaking Summit, AT&T and IndieWire teamed up again to celebrate the next generation of storytellers.
entry.content:
IndieWire and AT&T spent the month of October demonstrating our shared commitment to championing filmmakers and bringing untold stories to life.

First up was the IndieWire Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles, presented by AT&T, which assembled artists, executives, and thought leaders from every corner of the entertainment industry for a day of programming about where Hollywood is heading. Then a week later, we partnered to present the Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest, which celebrated the next generation of filmmakers who are bringing their visions to life.

Held at Ovation Hollywood on Saturday, October 25, the Filmmaker Party brought directors and festival attendees together for an evening of networking and movie discussions. The party even featured a complimentary headshot booth for anyone who wanted to take their career to the next level.

Related Stories
The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever
‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Is Lured Into Lily James’ Cult in a Gut-Wrenching Drama

The event was attended by “Honeyjoon” director Lilian Mehrel, who made her debut feature with the $1 million prize she won from the 2024 AT&T Untold Stories competition. She explained how the competition, which awards the biggest prize of its kind in the world, empowered her to tell a story that might not have otherwise found a home in the industry.

“Thank you to AT&T, to AFI Fest, and to everyone who champions filmmakers,” she said. “Because of you, more untold stories become told.”

Her comments echoed those of “Color Book” director David Fortune, who attended the Future of Filmmaking Summit to share his own experience from the life-changing competition.

Keep reading to see all the photos from the 2026 AFI Filmmaker Party, presented by AT&T and IndieWire.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen. For more information, visit here.

entry.title: The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever
entry.summary: When George Lazenby replaced Sean Connery in 1969, the result was a great James Bond movie that influenced Steven Soderbergh and Christopher Nolan.
entry.content:
When long-time producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped away from the James Bond franchise last year and Daniel Craig made it clear that he was finished playing agent 007, new producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman were faced with an unenviable task: finding a new actor to step into one of the most iconic roles in all of cinema. In the last few weeks, it’s been reported that Pascal, Heyman, and new Bond director Denis Villeneuve have zeroed in on a few final contenders including Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

Whoever the filmmakers choose, it’s likely to be controversial; Bond fans are very loyal to their particular favorites, and have been ever since Sean Connery was first replaced in the role back in 1969. The general consensus seems to be that Connery was the best Bond (though Craig runs a close second in most polls), but often one’s preference depends on which Bond was one’s first; as someone who grew up with Roger Moore, he’s always been my favorite, and I argued for his supremacy in an earlier IndieWire piece.

Related Stories
‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Is Lured Into Lily James’ Cult in a Gut-Wrenching Grief Drama
‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

The casting of a new James Bond has always set off a media furor, even in the days long before social media and Letterboxd. When Connery decided he had had enough as 007 after shooting the fifth James Bond movie, “You Only Live Twice,” the press followed producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman’s talent search with bated breath. Once the role was cast, they scrutinized the choice with an intensity that no actor could have survived — certainly not a male model whose only screen credit was a series of chocolate commercials.

After Connery quit, Broccoli, Saltzman, and director Peter Hunt spent over a year interviewing, auditioning, and screen testing hundreds of actors — including a young Shakespearean thespian named Timothy Dalton, who would go on to play Bond nearly 20 years later — to play Bond in “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” Anthony Rogers (“Camelot”), John Richardson (“Black Sunday”), and stage actor Roy Marsden were considered before the filmmakers landed on George Lazenby, whose previous acting experience was limited to those chocolate commercials.

Lazenby lied at his initial meeting and said he had been acting in movies Germany and Hong Kong, figuring the producers wouldn’t be able to check, but came clean to Hunt the next day. Hunt and the producers were concerned about Lazenby’s chops but loved his look, so they took a chance on the newcomer and put him through hours of voice coaching (to lose his Australian accent) and stunt training before deciding to pull the trigger a few weeks before production was scheduled to begin.

The question then became how to frame Lazenby’s onscreen introduction to make the transition as seamless as possible for audiences. One of screenwriter Richard Maibaum’s drafts began with Bond surviving an explosion that required him to undergo reconstructive surgery, but this was scrapped in favor of a more conventional prologue involving Bond encountering love interest Diana Rigg and fighting foes on the beach and in the water. When Rigg leaves Bond behind instead of making love to him as was customary for Bond’s leading ladies, Lazenby looks in the camera and says, “This never happened to the other fellow.”

It’s a very funny and very efficient way of acknowledging the change in personnel and then moving on, and the opening credit sequence further eases the transition by utilizing clips from earlier Bond movies. It also helps that the creative team on the movie consisted of Bond veterans including Maibaum, production designer Syd Cain, composer John Barry, and Hunt, who made his directorial debut with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had been an editor and second unit director on earlier Bond films.

As a result, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” still looks and sounds so much like a Bond film that the introduction of Lazenby is less jarring than it might have been, though what’s interesting about the movie is how much better it is in just about every way than the previous Connery pictures. One can argue about the relative merits of Connery vs. Lazenby, but there’s no debating the visual elegance of “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” which eschews the somewhat bland high-key lighting of the earlier Bond films in favor of something more atmospheric and glamorous.

Audiences at the time might not have appreciated Hunt and cinematographer Michael Reed’s efforts, being distracted by debates over Lazenby, but contemporary directors like Steven Soderbergh and Christopher Nolan have referenced “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” as an influence and made a case for it as the best of all James Bond movies. On his website, Soderbergh wrote that “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was cinematically “the best Bond film and the only one worth watching repeatedly for reasons other than pure entertainment (certainly it’s the only Bond film I look at and think: I’m stealing that shit).”

Aside from containing several of the series’ best set pieces (including some awe-inspiring ski chases that inspired Nolan when he made “Inception”), “On Her Majesty’s Service” is also the most emotionally resonant Bond film to be made before the Daniel Craig era, with a genuinely moving love story between Lazenby and Rigg. Although composer John Barry scored a lot of 007 movies, his talents were never put to better use than in this film, which fully took advantage of Barry’s skill for sweeping, romantic themes that would later win him an Oscar for “Out of Africa.”

Lazenby gets some of the credit here too; he may lack Connery’s icy charm, but he’s a more human Bond. Displaying a slightly goofier sense of humor than Connery, he’s a transitional figure between the original 007 and the more overtly comic one Roger Moore would introduce in “Live and Let Die” four years later. According to Lazenby, he could have expressed even more emotion had Peter Hunt allowed it; when the actor played one particularly devastating scene with tears in his eyes, Hunt ordered a second take, arguing that Bond shouldn’t cry.

As good as he is in the part, Lazenby’s experience shooting “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” doesn’t seem to have been pleasurable, though whether or not the blame rests on his shoulders depends on who’s telling the story. According to Lazenby, Hunt went cold toward him early in shooting over a misunderstanding and was too preoccupied with the technical side of things to give him much attention; Cubby Broccoli, on the other hand, said Lazenby was spoiled and entitled and alienated many of his colleagues.

Although Broccoli was ultimately happy with Lazenby’s performance, by the time the movie opened, there were a lot of lingering hard feelings — a situation that wasn’t helped by the fairly lukewarm reviews Lazenby received, or by one of his representatives making a statement that Lazenby would not be returning to the role of James Bond. This was the first Broccoli or Harry Saltzman heard of any plans for Lazenby to abandon the part, and they quickly announced that Lazenby had been fired to make it seem as though his departure was their decision, not his.

Although Lazenby later stressed that he wasn’t the one who made the announcement he was quitting, he also clearly didn’t have any great desire to stay on as Bond. His contract was for seven years and had multiple clauses that he felt would restrict his career and lifestyle, and he still hadn’t signed it when “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” wrapped. Lazenby figured he could make more money doing one film in Italy than he could in five years on his Bond contract; he also, in one of the great errors in judgment in movie history, assumed that the James Bond franchise was dying in the era of “Easy Rider” and wouldn’t last much longer anyway.

In fact, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was a sizable hit, grossing $82 million on a production budget of $8 million. It wasn’t as popular as the last Connery film, however, and the mixed reviews gave it the aura of a failure. Broccoli and Saltzman began another worldwide search for a new Bond, considering American stars like Clint Eastwood, Burt Reynolds, and Adam West before convincing Connery to return. The result, “Diamonds Are Forever,” was a monster hit, and Lazenby went on to scattered work around Europe, acknowledging years later that his decision to quit Bond was a major mistake.

Lazenby didn’t completely leave 007 behind, however. After “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” he played a James Bond-esque character in the “Alfred Hitchcock Presents” episode “Diamonds Aren’t Forever” and, in 1983, Lazenby appeared in the TV movie “Return of the Man from U.N.C.L.E.” as a spy with the initials J.B. (who drove an Aston Martin, no less). The actor made a handful of interesting films after he played Bond, most notably Brian Trenchard-Smith’s great action film “The Man from Hong Kong” and Peter Bogdanovich’s exquisite Paul Theroux adaptation “Saint Jack.”

Lazenby was never more memorable than he was as James Bond, however, and it’s a shame he didn’t play the character in more pictures and further develop his variations on the persona. It remains to be seen where Villeneuve’s selection will place in the pantheon of Bonds, but whoever is cast would best be advised to ignore the inevitable social media firestorm that’s coming their way.

Lazenby’s saga proves that no matter how capable an actor is stepping into Bond’s shoes, it takes a while for history to render a fair assessment. 57 years after critics dismissed it, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” has stood the test of time — it’s Soderbergh and Nolan’s verdicts, not those of the contemporary press, that have proven correct.

entry.title: ‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Is Lured Into Lily James’ Cult in a Gut-Wrenching Grief Drama
entry.summary: The fall festival hit opens in theaters on January 8. Watch the trailer for 'The Liberation.'
entry.content:
Few prospects excite us more at IndieWire than news of a new Carrie Coon performance, and the actress’ upcoming turn in Guy Nattiv‘s “The Liberation” gives her one of the meatiest characters of her career. The film has already played at several major fall festivals, including Telluride and Toronto, launching Coon into the heart of the Best Actress race — but we won’t complain about watching it again when it hits theaters this winter, courtesy of Bleecker Street.

An official synopsis for “The Liberation” reads “Rita (Carrie Coon), a woman in midlife haunted by the weight of her past, encounters magnetic young spiritual leader Ricki (Lily James) and leaves her family to follow her to an all-female commune. But when her daughters Ella (Bella Ramsey) and Jo (Odessa Young) arrive unexpectedly and become drawn into the group’s seductive world, Rita is forced to choose between the family she left behind and the life she believes can save her.”

Related Stories
‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way
‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses

When IndieWire’s Kate Erbland reviewed the film out of TIFF, she singled out Coon’s rich performance as a clear high point of the film.

“Rita has long felt like she was standing on the outside of her life, and the brief flashes we see of the joy the group (before it so clearly becomes a cult) elicits in her, the feeling she is part of something, is profound,” the review reads. “It makes her later time in the cult so much worse, with a slack-jawed, blank-staring Naia trying to tell her kids that no, no, things are really great, she’s happier than she’s ever been, this is what she wants. That she needs to be freed from this is a bit of a given, but ‘The Liberation’ gently pokes holes in the idea that her “outside” life is so much better. Perhaps there is no place for Rita in this world, a horrific revelation that Coon’s performance drives home with significant power.”

The film’s theatrical release is just a couple months away, but if you can’t wait that long to get your Carrie Coon fix, check out her recent appearance on IndieWire’s Screen Talk podcast, where she discussed her performance in the film as well as her larger career.

Bleecker Street will release “The Liberation” in theaters on Friday, January 8. Watch the trailer below.

entry.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way
entry.summary: Godzilla squares off against King Ghidorah in an IMAX-sized melodrama that features some of the most thrilling kaiju fights ever.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 26, 2026 at the 2026 New York Film Festival. GKIDS will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Asked to explain the goofy title he gave to his globally successful 2023 kaiju smash “Godzilla Minus One,” writer-director Takashi Yamazaki explained that it was meant to convey two co-equal things: 1.) That the movie took place before Ishirō Honda’s original “Godzilla,” and 2.) That “people rise up from a postwar Japan that is at zero, and then Godzilla arrives, making the situation even worse and more tragic.”

Continuing the story of its Oscar-winning predecessor while also doubling down on everything that made it the most acclaimed film in its franchise since the King of the Monsters first lumbered out of the Pacific Ocean in 1954, Yamazaki’s thunderously loud and frequently spectacular direct sequel has in turn been saddled with an even sillier title: “Godzilla Minus Zero.” To paraphrase the scene from “Sideways” where Paul Giamatti’s character reveals that his novel is called “The Day After Yesterday”: Isn’t that just… “Godzilla?”

Related Stories
‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses
‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale

Yes and no. Sure, the title is absurd on its face, but — in keeping with Yamazaki’s logic — it also rather eloquently speaks to the premise of a film about a fragile people who are struggling to maintain (and build upon) the new equilibrium they’ve fought so hard to achieve in the years since their country became the epicenter of Earth’s nuclear era. Another mid-century melodrama with very occasional monster sightings, the more thematically coherent and emotionally affecting “Godzilla Minus Zero” expands on the naive grassroots nationalism of its predecessor by reframing that movie’s characters from victims to survivors, an emphasis that forces ex-kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) and his friends to confront a series of impossible questions. How do you balance grief with growth? Vengeance with peace? Self-sacrifice with self-preservation?

By way of answering those questions (or at least asking them in a variety of increasingly anguished ways), “Godzilla Minus Zero” also forces Shikishima and co. to confront a flying, IMAX-sized, three-headed asshole they come to know as King Ghidorah. Possibly the single most hateable kaiju who’s ever eaten innocent civilians on screen before, King Ghidorah is a real piece of work even before he earns his crown. He first rears his ugly dragon head in Matsumoto circa 1949, which is two years after the events of “Godzilla Minus One,” and maybe two weeks after this scaly destroyer of worlds crash-landed into the mountains of Japan on the back of a meteorite (an arbitrary point of origin that feels like a missed opportunity to freight Ghidora with more human-facing pathos). Seeing as how Godzilla was obliterated and left to rot at the bottom of the sea at the end of the previous film, Ghidora is free to terrorize the countryside whenever he isn’t taking cute little naps in the Nagano hills.

Lucky for Japan, and for all of the other nations that are still living under the delusion that none of this monster business will ever be their problem, at least one of the key heroes who “defeated” Godzilla in 1947 has been preparing his people for the possibility of another kaiju attack. Government higher-ups are still nowhere to be seen, but Einstein-haired Naval engineer Noda (a sweet and eccentrically professorial Hidetaka Yoshioka) has been appointed to the head of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, where he’s joined by newcomer Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a preternaturally gifted meteorologist whose ability to predict the weather proves crucial in the fight against Ghidorah, and also embittered biologist Kanji Murakami (“Twilight Samurai” star Min Tanaka), who survived the bombing of Hiroshima, the attack on Ginza in “Godzilla Minus One,” and the assault on Matsumoto that opens this film — a detail that evokes the terribly remarkable story of Tsutomo Yamaguchi.

Thanks to Noda’s hard-earned wisdom, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is able to skip over the part where everyone has to discover that kaiju like Ghidorah are immune to conventional weapons — if not also strengthened by them. That ignorance is reserved for the occupying Americans, who were entirely absent from the previous movie (which nostalgically privileged the self-reliance of Japan’s civilian population at the expense of a more historical view of the post-war struggle). Here, the U.S. Army is represented by a unit of square-jawed, power-hungry jerks who are only interested in helping Japan so far as it helps themselves. They don’t bear the wounds of nuclear devastation, and so they see kaiju as more of an opportunity than a threat.

The opposite is true for our pal Shikishima, who has absolutely no interest in ever climbing back into the cockpit of a fight plane. Now married to the angelic Noriko — Minami Hamabe, who miraculously escaped “Godzilla Minus One” with a new eyepatch and some big secrets — and embracing his role as adoptive father to the devastatingly cute Akiko (returning champion Sae Nagatani), Shikishima just wants to wear his cool brown leather jacket and messenger bag combo in peace.

If only it were that simple. If only Shikishima were convinced, as he tries to convince himself, that staying out of the fight is the best way to protect the women he loves. If only Noda’s plan of electrocuting Ghidorah to death in the skies above Matsumoto were as successful at killing the kaiju as it is at blowing our hair back.

There are only two sustained monster sequences in “Minus Zero,” which adheres to a similar cadence as its predecessor, but they’re both among the most gripping setpieces of their kind in all of moviedom; they match the grandeur — if not the majesty — of those from Gareth Edwards’ “Godzilla,” and eclipse their violent intensity. The ridiculously thrilling aerial sequence above Matsumoto is lifted by the Wagnerian strings of Naoki Satō’s visceral score, kept aloft by special effects that exponentially improve upon the resourceful but weightless CGI from “Minus One,” and seared into your retinas by IMAX razzledazzle of the highest magnitude. And while the final showdown between Ghidorah and Godzilla is slightly weakened by grayscale atmospherics and a few missing beats (one of them very bizarre), it goes without saying that the climatic brawl is one for the ages, as Yamazaki earns the franchise’s first “R” rating with an elegantly choreographed monster mash that rattles with Darwinian force.

Oh yeah, I suppose it also goes without saying that Godzilla is (eventually) in this Godzilla movie. Somehow, the King of the Monsters has returned — if Palpatine had infinitely regenerative flesh, perhaps his resurrection would have been similarly unsurprising. But fans of Honda’s original film, Yamazaki’s previous one, and/or Edwards’ failed 2014 reboot have come to expect and appreciate that Godzilla is most effective when framed as more of a recurring weather phenomenon than a dramatic engine in his own right, and “Godzilla Minus Zero” doesn’t suffer from its title kaiju’s limited screentime.

On the contrary, his absences are crucial to the construction of a florid tear-jerker about a traumatized country trying to move forward in the atomic shadow of a world that will never feel safe again. While a cursed biologist like Murakami might see vengeance as his only path towards peace, a former kamikaze like Shikishima — the guilt he once felt over not killing himself for Japan now bent towards the responsibility he feels towards living for Noriko and their daughter — is left to wrestle over the best way to protect his family: fighting the monsters, or fleeing from them.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is hardly the most nuanced or effective film to explore its country’s post-war despair (the original “Godzilla” still towers above it in that regard, to say nothing of “Drunken Angel,” “The Human Condition,” “An Inn at Osaka,” or any number of other cornerstones of Japanese cinema), but the anger it assigns to Murakami is provocative on its own terms, and the path that it contrives for Shikishima is considerably more nuanced and well-earned than the one he stumbled through before. While the future is still uncertain by the end of this latest Godzilla movie (which feels very much like the middle chapter of a trilogy), “Minus Zero” makes rewarding sense of why the series’ numbers are starting to add up.

Grade: B+

“Godzilla Minus Zero” premiered at the 2026 New York Film Festival. GKIDS will release it in U.S. theaters on Friday, November 6.

entry.title: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses
entry.summary: Lionsgate is partnering with Facebook parent company Meta on a 3D version of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' for its VR glasses.
entry.content:
Lionsgate‘s “Hunger Games” prequel “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” will be available in 3D when it opens in theaters on November 20. That on its own isn’t strictly news, but the 3D conversion on the film is coming from a new and unlikely place: Facebook parent company Meta.

Meta is partnering with Lionsgate to convert “Sunrise on the Reaping” to 3D, with director Francis Lawrence working to adapt the film for 3D viewing. Meta worked with VFX giant DNEG and their internal 3D conversion branch Stereo. This is the first time Meta has partnered with a Hollywood film studio on such an undertaking, and it also won’t be the last Lionsgate movie that will get the 3D treatment down the road (other titles will be announced at a later date).

Related Stories
‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale
‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser

In addition to “Sunrise on the Reaping” being in 3D in theaters, the movie will eventually be available on Meta VR Glasses when those VR devices hit the shelves in spring 2027. IndieWire got to demo those recently, and they’re designed to be lighter and less obtrusive than other VR headsets that can be tougher on the eyes while not sacrificing any of the immersive qualities (they feel and look like slightly larger sunglasses that you might get at the dentist rather than a bulky, wraparound headset that weighs on your face).

The demo we saw included a snippet of the Billie Eilish concert doc co-directed by James Cameron, as well as a clip from “Avengers: Endgame” that added an extra expanded screen effect to fill your line of sight. It’s clear that Meta wants to expand into the entertainment space and compete with the likes of YouTube and Google and other tech giants, and they need premium content like a new “Hunger Games” movie in order to do that.

“From the beginning, we wanted ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ to feel visceral and immersive, pulling audiences deep into Haymitch’s experience,” Lawrence said in a statement. “Adapting the film for 3D gave us another creative tool to bring audiences even closer to his perspective. I’m excited for people to see the film on the big screen and ultimately experience it in an entirely new way on Meta’s VR glasses.”

“As we continue to explore new ways for audiences to experience ‘The Hunger Games,’ we’re thrilled to partner with Meta on this first-of-its-kind collaboration,” said Jim Packer, Chief Revenue Officer, Lionsgate. “Francis Lawrence has created an incredible 3D experience for ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ and we’re excited for audiences to experience it in theaters and then on Meta VR Glasses. This is a compelling example of how technology can transform existing formats to create fresh, new experiences.”

“With our upcoming VR Glasses, we’re proud to create premium entertainment the way it’s meant to be felt, and Lionsgate is an ideal partner because of the artistic strength and global appeal of its franchises,” said Sarah Malkin, Head of Entertainment for Meta’s Reality Labs. “’The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ is exactly the kind of cinematic experience that will be phenomenal in theaters, and also showcases what this technology makes possible at home. We’re delighted to work with Lionsgate and Francis Lawrence to bring the film in 3D to audiences around the world.”

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is the sixth “Hunger Games” film and the second prequel after “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” from 2023, which brought in $363 million at the worldwide box office. This film stars Joseph Zada as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy, who is the District 12 character portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original series of films. The film also stars McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., and Ben Wang.

entry.title: ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale
entry.summary: Kelly O'Sullivan and Alex Thompson's third production together, 'Mouse,' is another gem, and might be their best effort to date. Berlin review.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on February 13, 2026 at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. IFC Films will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6.]

For the final 20 or so minutes of an early screening of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson‘s Berlin-bound “Mouse” that I recently attended, the woman sitting behind me in one of NYC’s smallest screening rooms sobbed. Like, really sobbed. I could hear her gasps in between her cries. Yes, I thought to myself, one of my people.

While I’m not sure there’s yet a cult assembled around the deeply empathetic and uniquely humane cinema of O’Sullivan and Thompson (partners in both film and life), God willing, there will be after more audiences see the pair’s third effort. I’ve been banging the drum on their wondrous output since 2020’s “Saint Frances” (which Thompson directed and O’Sullivan wrote and starred in) and their deep-feeling follow-up, 2024’s “Ghostlight” (written by O’Sullivan, who also joined Thompson in co-directing duties). Around these parts, any O’Sullivan and Thompson joint is an event.

Related Stories
‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser
IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’

“Mouse” is no exception, and their best effort yet.

As is typically the case with the pair’s films, its logline does not quite do it justice. “Saint Frances” was about a disaffected nanny who bonds with her young charge. “Ghostlight” followed a fractured family as they found unexpected healing in live theater. “Mouse” is about a shy high school senior looking for ballast after the sudden end of her lifelong BFF-ship. These are all “small” stories, but they are also crucially about people, and thus contain the wild multitudes of humanity itself.

O’Sullivan and Thompson reunite with their “Ghostlight” star, Katherine Mallen Kupferer (whose own parents starred alongside her in the previous feature), who is cast here as our titular Mouse. Well, sort of. Her name is Minnie, but her shyness leans toward the mousy, though no one would ever say that to her, least of all her beloved and extremely outgoing best friend, Callie (Chloe Coleman). But when Minnie’s itchy nickname is (wrongly, it turns out) attributed to the flashy Callie, it’s hard for her to shake its deeper meanings.

When the film opens, Minnie and Callie are wrapping their final day as high school juniors in the early summer of 2002 (cue the Michelle Branch soundtrack, perfect). The stage is being set for their senior year — and, quite literally, for the very talented Callie’s next big high school musical moment and her eventual plans to attend Juilliard — and it’s obvious that they’re not about to have the same experience. Callie is popular and vivacious, perpetually surrounded by admirers and various hangers-on (Audrey Grace Marshall’s Cara is hellbent on usurping Minnie’s place in Callie’s life, while her himbo-esque boyfriend Brad is given wonderful dimension through Beck Nolan’s sneaky-good performance).

Minnie? She’s much more reserved, orbiting around Callie and company, not quite ever the star of her own show. But this is not a story about two best friends who break up because of the vagaries of popularity, and Coleman’s Callie is not a villain who breaks Minnie’s delicate heart. Well, not on purpose.

It’s clear that Minnie is out of touch with lots about her life — though not her affection for Callie — including her own sexuality (Iman Vellani as cute local video store clerk Kat happily cracks through that) and her fraught relationship with her overworked mother (Mallen Kupferer’s own mom and “Ghostlight” co-star, Tara Mallen). Callie’s friendship and trust are the best things in her life. Her nice house with a fully stocked kitchen is a bonus, as is Callie’s very-put-together mom Helen (a heartbreaking Sophie Okonedo), who wisely seems to like the steady Minnie a whole heck of a lot more than the rest of Callie’s coterie.

That will prove to be the one saving grace of what comes next. When Minnie and Callie’s friendship comes to a sudden end, it’s only through bonding with Helen that Minnie finds any sort of ballast in her life. But as point-A-to-point-B as that might sound, O’Sullivan and Thompson remain uniquely attuned to the ebbs and flows of real life and how real people respond to it. Mallen Kupferer, so outspoken in “Ghostlight” and so wonderfully goofy in “Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret,” here sinks into the far harder-to-crack Minnie. That’s not to say that Minnie isn’t prone to the emotional wilds of any teenage girl, but the young actress’ finely tuned performance is never broad or silly.

Instead, we get to know Minnie during one of the worst times of her life. So too does Helen, who handles her own feelings about Callie through her own coping mechanisms, some of which work, most of which don’t, and many of which center on building her own friendship with Minnie. The pair of them has a lot in common beyond Callie, including a general sense of wisdom beyond their years that has not always been beneficial to them.

Early in the film, Cara insists that Callie’s group of friends (including both Cara and Minnie) partake in a horrific little parlor game she likens to “Personal Feedback.” Mostly, it’s an excuse for the teenagers to say terrible things about each other under the guise of honesty and friendship. Even our golden girl, Callie, doesn’t escape unharmed, though Minnie almost does, because Cara simply can’t be bothered to remember she exists.

“Mouse” is, at its heart, a wonderful rebuttal to just that sort of cruel thinking — for all the Minnies out there — and a reminder that everyone matters and everyone deserves to be seen. Lofty as that might sound, it’s one of the most basic tenets of humanity, and the kind of thing too often forgotten on the big screen. O’Sullivan and Thompson never forget, however, and their films reflect exactly that. Our only request: more, please, our people need this.

Grade: A-

“Mouse” premiered at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival.

entry.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser
entry.summary: Peter Farrelly continues his reign of making audience-delighting hits for the TIFF crowd, but this one pulls its punches a bit. 'I Love Rocky' review.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 13, 2026 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.]

You’re going to see the hits coming with this one. When Anthony Ippolito first utters the title of Peter Farrelly‘s “I Play Rocky” — it’s an admission and an ask, a demand and a plea — the moment is primed for stand-up-and-cheer crowd-pleasing. Such is the case with Farrelly’s entire film, which tracks Sylvester Stallone’s wild, improbable Hollywood success story through the lens of his creation of “Rocky,” often functioning as its own version of that underdog story, presumably because “Rocky” proper isn’t available to be remade and Stallone was not formally involved with the production of this one.

Related Stories
IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’
‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year

Stallone has long mythologized his rise to greatness, and that’s no knock on him; his rise to Hollywood royalty was crazy and filled with eye-popping twists and turns. The guy sold his dog when he didn’t have enough money! But Peter Gamble’s script sands down those hard edges into something much more made-for-the-movies, a distinctly knotty treatment for a movie that is meant to be about how hard it is to get original movies made.

While the lightness of the film — including an awkward dinner in which Frank Stallone, Jr. (Matt Dillon) giddily admits to beating his kid, mostly played for chuckles — can detract from the much darker stuff that really happened to Stallone, it’s hard to deny the power of a feature so genuinely built to delight. You can see the strings being pulled (the ropes being strung?), but that means it works more often than not. With a big crowd — a man behind me at the film’s second public screening at TIFF guffawed and hooted with such abandon throughout the film that I could only embrace his joy — “I Play Rocky” does exactly what it’s trying to do.

It doesn’t do much more, though.

Stallone’s life story has been threaded through the period just before he started writing scripts and the opening night of “Rocky,” an essential time in the career of a man so dedicated to acting and his craft that it could have ruined him forever. And there’s some light ruin here, including a short stint sleeping on the street (we see literally one night), bonkers financial decisions, and grievous financial choices. Embodied to an almost disarming degree by actor Anthony Ippolito — most people are probably going to get hung up on his impersonation of Stallone’s signature voice, but I’ve never seen anyone make their cheekbones look like Sly’s unexpectedly sunken ones — what feels most real about the film exists because he’s so fully committed to the bit.

And it’s very much to the breakout star’s credit that it doesn’t feel like a bit. While Gamble’s script doesn’t get much further than “this dude just really loved acting,” Ippolito gets pretty soulful here. His Sly (or, as we first meet him during a run of demeaning auditions, “Mike”) is a striver who would likely never call himself “ambitious.” Self-taught, self-educated, and self-aware to a fault, Sly knows he’s not the ideal Hollywood star, but he’s hellbent on showing the world what he’s got.

When his eventual first wife Sasha (a wonderfully calm AnnaSophia Robb) encourages him to just “write a fricking script” worthy of his talents, he does. The first is not “Rocky.” Neither are the seven that follow, but Sly and Sasha still pull up stakes for Hollywood and to chase his dream. No one is buying what he’s selling, though, and even some promising meetings (including one with Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff, both played to the absolute hilt by P.J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell, respectively) end nowhere. A chance encounter — the film’s script lives and dies by those — with a seminal boxing match gives him fresh inspiration, and after just three days, the kid has “Rocky.”

But is he going to be Rocky? Of course, everyone on Earth who sees this film (and plenty who don’t) knows that answer, but what the film lacks in tension, it makes up for in pure grit. Sly learns all about Hollywood negotiations, blustery studio men (a role Tracy Letts was born to play; no one has more fun yelling “Fuck Paramount!” than this guy), and holding fast to seriously deluded dreams. And while the film can flag as we chug through those paces, once “Rocky” is greenlit with Sly in the lead role (and a mess of stipulations, all of them seemingly designed to trip him up), things really start zipping along.

Part of that is due to smart casting. Jay Duplass is a stellar pick for director John G. Avildsen, though anyone who knows anything about Stallone’s on-set approach will chuckle at how much these two seemed to get along (Stephan James should get his own Carl Weathers film now). But more of it comes from the film’s eventual bent toward the mechanics of moviemaking. Come for the high jinks involving beating back union reps (but also, ew?), stay for a subplot about the genius of the Steadicam that is genuinely moving to observe.

That “Rocky” will be a hit is a given — and a fricking huge one at that! — but “I Play Rocky” is far more invested in getting the audience on board with the road it took to get there. And while Farrelly’s approach to this material, extremely glossy and built to delight a wide array of audience members, doesn’t quite speak to the real pain that went into the making of “Rocky,” there’s still plenty here that will make people stand up and cheer. It would, however, be nice if this Hollywood story didn’t feel quite so, well, Hollywood.

Grade: B-

“I Play Rocky” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide later in the month.

entry.title: IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’
entry.summary: IndieWire's Trevor Wallace has won a Daytime Emmy for editing our IndieWire Craft Roundtables series.
entry.content:
IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace is officially an Emmy winner.

Wallace won the Editing for a Daytime Studio Program category at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys for his work on Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables.” He accepted the award during the ceremony at the Hollywood Palladium on Friday, October 30.

IndieWire was also nominated for a Daytime Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Daytime Studio Non-Fiction Series for IndieWire executive producer Mary Pelloni’s work on the show. The two nominations and one win, in categories that also included broadcast talk shows, reflect IndieWire’s increasing presence in the traditional video spaces in addition to our written coverage.

Related Stories
‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year
Netflix Will Give Joel Coen’s Gothic Mystery ‘Jack of Spades’ a Theatrical Release in 2027

Wallace works on IndieWire’s staff as a video producer, where he also produces and edits video content across brands like Filmmaker Toolkit, Future of Filmmaking, and other editorial and sponsored projects.

Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables” highlighted the below-the-line artisans on many of the biggest films of the season. Hosted by IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill, the season consisted of four episodes, each centered around a different filmmaking department: cinematography, editing, production design, and casting. Each episode aired on PBS SoCal and streamed on the PBS App in addition to editorial coverage on IndieWire.com.

Wallace won for the editing roundtable episode, which featured included editors Kirk Baxter (“A House of Dynamite”), Affonso Goncalves (“Hamnet”), Michael P. Shawver (“Sinners”), Andy Jurgensen (“One Battle After Another”), Pamela Martin (“Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere”), Saar Klein (“Dead Man’s Wire”), and Luke Lynch (“BLKNWS: Terms & Conditions”).

The cinematography roundtable featured Adolpho Veloso (“Train Dreams”), Malik Hassan Sayeed (“After the Hunt”), Michael Bauman (“One Battle After Another”), and William Rexer (“The Testament of Ann Lee”).

The production design roundtable featured conversations with Cara Brower (“Hedda”), Sam Bader (“The Testament of Ann Lee”), Alexandra Schaller (“Train Dreams”), Scott Chambliss (“Kiss of the Spider Woman”), and Dylan Cole and Ben Procter (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”).

The casting roundtable also featured casting directors Nina Gold (“Jay Kelly”), Margery Simkin (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”), and Jessica Ronane (“After the Hunt”).

“IndieWire Craft Roundtables” returned for Season 2 in June 2026, with six episodes devoted to the biggest TV shows of the year.

entry.title: ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year
entry.summary: The "30 Rock" team has made something new while adhering to their joke-dense, pop-culture savvy, and network-friendly approach to sitcoms.
entry.content:
When I first thought, “Is ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ the funniest show on television?”, I worried saying as much would be damning the uproarious NBC sitcom with faint praise. After all, the modern TV landscape is awash with crime shows, genre mash-ups, and I.P. brand extensions. Bad comedies abound (and tend to be mercifully easy to spot), but great ones? Hmm. At least the most recent Emmy winner for Best Comedy Series is an actual comedy, but the nominees (including a feel-good weeper, a rom-com heavy on the rom, and that cooking drama) were still emblematic of a Hollywood era when laughs aren’t the top priority.

Related Stories
As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually
‘Who Killed Alex Odeh?’ Review: A Scattered but Searing Documentary Examines America’s Tacit Acceptance of Anti-Arab Discrimination

So, returning to the original question, how many funny funny shows actually came out this year?

Turns out, quite a few. “Adults” jumps to mind among recent releases for its successful Season 2 evolution into a hang-worthy Gen-Z hangout sitcom. “Colin From Accounts” capped a three-year run that saw the Aussie romantic-comedy get stronger every season. “Youth” has Sharon Horgan back at the top of her game (let’s not speak of “Bad Sisters” Season 2), and “The Comeback” did the impossible by delivering a worthy successor to one of HBO’s greatest-ever TV seasons. Then there’s trusty comedy staples like “It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia” and “Abbott Elementary,” which don’t need another crossover to keep us laughing, as well as the half-comedies that feel full to anyone with the same funny bone, like “The Lowdown” (a noir comedy), “The Audacity” (a black-comic drama), and “Trying” (a family comedy). I didn’t even mention the final season of “Hacks” (which is great) or the first (and hopefully final) season of “The Hawk” (which is not).

“Reggie Dinkins” tops them all.

Following fallen NFL running back Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan), decades after he’s ousted from the league for gambling, Season 2 picks up amid incremental progress toward his crowning redemption: making the Pro Football Hall of Fame. His documentarian, Arthur Tobin (Daniel Radcliffe), is still searching for the right angle to support their comeback film (Arthur needs it as much as Reggie wants it), while Reggie’s agent and ex-wife Monica (Erika Alexander) tries to build on the little momentum they gained at the end of last season (when Reggie earned his first votes ever).

The irresistible ensemble doesn’t have a weak link. The staging is vibrant. The writing is as happy to delve into topical subject matter (like documentary subjects paying their documentarians) as it is to revel in carefree absurdity (like a harebrained murder-conspiracy or calamitous Thanksgiving gathering). And every element of it is always focused on being funny. Not only is Robert Carlock and Sam Means’ NBC sitcom designed to squeeze in as many jokes as the human brain can process in 21-minute chunks, it’s also carefully paced and polished to keep those jokes as superb and surprising as possible.

Take a check-your-phone-and-you’ll-miss-it gag from the Season 2 premiere: Monica is struggling to keep up with the media landscape’s sprawling marketing opportunities and admits she booked Reggie on the wrong show: She mixed up Pablo Torres’ sports podcast with Julio Torres’ “something.” Quick cut to Julio (as himself) interviewing Reggie about “the color clear.” There’s a laugh in recognizing Monica’s mistake, another laugh in Julio’s question (“What do you think about the color clear?”), and another laugh in Reggie’s response (“A lot!”).

But rather than one joke stepping on the next, they amplify one another. Monica’s explanation is given the most space to land, since technically it’s setting up the cutaway jokes to come. Those jokes hit one after the next, but in a rhythm that makes them easy to process independently. They’re calibrated to keep you laughing all the way through, but they’re not so rushed that you feel overwhelmed instead of entertained.

That’s the magic (or maybe the math) behind what’s recognized as Tina Fey (an EP on “Dinkins”) and Robert Carlock’s comedy style, as established by their landmark sitcom, “30 Rock” and extended more successfully than not in comedies like “Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt” (where they picked up Radcliffe), “Great News,” “Mr. Mayor,” and “Girls5Eva.” Carlock continues it here with Means, who worked on all those shows, while relying on their proven bonds with Morgan, Radcliffe, and stealth MVP Bobby Moynihan to maintain the right balance. (Moynihan’s understanding of tone and timing is impeccable, and he’s such a joyful presence it’s hard not to smile whenever Rusty surfaces.)

The Season 2 premiere illustrates the trust the writers’ have in their entire acting company. The story still pivots around Morgan’s lovable doofus, but the emphasis is elsewhere. Arthur is dying for the family to find out about Reggie’s son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall) and his secret relationship with Delilah Basmati (Arica Himmel), daughter of Reggie’s nemesis, Jerry Basmati (Craig Robinson). Brina (Precious Way) gets close, while Monica is busy hiring a new assistant “head of publicity” to help her tap into younger markets with a broader reach. Moynihan’s Rusty is everywhere, chipping in enough quips, reaction shots, and physical comedy to convey his supportive yet integral presence in each character’s life.

By the time our original dynamic duo gets a cathartic moment near the episode’s end, it’s hard not to notice that Reggie and Arthur almost feel like an afterthought — and that’s just fine. They take back control in the ensuing episodes, after “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” proves it can thrive no matter who gets to press the most buttons. The joke-delivery machine is operating at peak volume, and it needs every capable hand to keep its performance at the same incredible sweep.

With only four episodes screened for review, there’s plenty of time for Season 2 to break down. The charming vibe could fade, the sharp jokes could soften, the elastic performances could calcify. But not only does Carlock and co.’s lengthy track record suggest the opposite trajectory, so does the excitement shown in creating this specific project. You can feel it in the ideas, big and small, throughout “The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins,” and their cumulative impact makes the series special — not because of a general dearth in great comedies, or even because it harkens back to an era of Must-See TV, when multiple classic sitcoms airing on the same night spoiled viewers with an abundance of laughs. It’s just because laughing this hard, this often, is a gift. And there’s nothing faint about it.

Grade: A-

“The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins” Season 2 premieres Monday, November 2 at 8:30 p.m. ET on NBC. New episodes will be released weekly and made available on Peacock the next day.

entry.title: Netflix Will Give Joel Coen’s Gothic Mystery ‘Jack of Spades’ a Theatrical Release in 2027
entry.summary: The film stars Patsy Ferran, Josh O’Connor, Damian Lewis, and Lesley Manville.
entry.content:
Joel Coen is heading back to Netflix. After taking his 2021 “The Tragedy of Macbeth” to A24, the filmmaker is bringing his latest solo directorial outing back to Netflix, where he last teamed with brother Ethan Coen on the 2018 release “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.” Rest assured, however, while Ethan is not sharing directing duties with his big brother again, he did co-write the film‘s script alongside Joel, novelist and screenwriter Eleanor Catton, and playwright and screenwriter Conor McPherson.

The new film is called “Jack of Spades,” and the streamer will give it a theatrical release in the fall of 2027 ahead of its debut on Netflix. The film is based on Frances Frederica Montrésor’s 1901 novel “The Alien: A Story of Middle Age” and its official logline reads: “A sinister gothic mystery filled with intrigue and betrayal set in the atmospheric Scottish Highlands.”

Related Stories
As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually
‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival

The film will star Olivier Award winner Patsy Ferran, BAFTA nominee and Golden Globe winner Josh O’Connor, BAFTA nominee and Golden Globe winner Damian Lewis, and Oscar nominee Lesley Manville.

The book itself is billed as “a thoughtful pick for readers who enjoy character-driven fiction with a touch of wanderlust and a battle between integrity and longing.” Montrésor’s novel follows Esther Mordaunt, “now well into her thirties by the story’s start” and “follows her evolving bond with Jasper, a traveler with a vivid past and a talent for storytelling. Through his tales of sailing, revolutions, and distant lands, the book explores how a single life can stretch across time, risk, and longing without losing its humanity.”

Coen will also reunite with Oscar-nominated cinematographer Bruno Delbonnel (“Inside Llewyn Davis”) and composer Carter Burwell (“Fargo,” “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs”). The film will be produced by Robert Graf, Frances McDormand, Coen, Steven Rales, Graham Broadbent, and Pete Czernin, and executive produced by Donald MacKinnon.

entry.title: As Production Jobs Flee California, Governor Gavin Newsom Pushes to Expand Film and TV Tax Credit to $1 Billion Annually
entry.summary: As California production jobs dry up, Gov. Newsom pushes to expand film and TV tax credit from $750 million to $1 billion.
entry.content:
Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing expanding California’s current film and television tax credit program from $750 million to at least $1 billion annually as the state is struggling to attract entertainment industry jobs. The move comes as a report last month by FilmLA found that production levels fell 3.7 percent in the third quarter even as California has continued to enhance its tax credits. Many of the major studios and streamers are headquartered in Los Angeles, which makes the contraction in production jobs more painful.

Last year, Gov. Newsom pushed to increase California’s film and TV incentive from $330 million to $750 million annually, and the state’s film commission saw an initial rise in applications before the number of productions began falling again. California is not only grappling with increased competition from states like New Jersey, New York, and Georgia that offer richer incentives, but they are also facing off against foreign production hubs such as the United Kingdom and Hungary.

Related Stories
‘Earthlings in Love’ Review: A Sentimental Sci-fi Journey Makes the Leap from TikTok to the Tokyo International Film Festival
Ruth Madeley Never Thought Acting Was an Option — Now, She’s Playing a Disability Rights Legend in ‘Being Heumann’

In a press release, Gov. Newsom said the proposed expansion would include credits for above-the-line talent, as well as rewards for companies that commit to fielding more than one production in California. If enacted, the tax credit will be extended through 2040, which would give companies more certainty about the incentives they can access. The previous incentives were scheduled to last through 2030. It would also increase independent film funding to $100 million annually, up $26 million from the current program.

“California created the modern entertainment industry; we’re the capital of entertainment and we’re going to keep it here,” Newsom said in a statement. “At least $1 billion in tax credits means more investment flowing into our economy and more opportunity across the industry. Through this expansion, we will maintain the momentum and success of our historic expansion last year.”

The governor also urged national lawmakers to pass a federal film and television incentive, which could augment states’ efforts to bolster local production.

“States can’t shoulder the cost alone, which is why I am calling on Congress to back up an expanded tax credit by passing national film and TV tax credit legislation already on the table,” Newsom said.
